statute.section: Section 74 — Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for
statute.text: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

authorities.cite: Kailash Nath Associates v Delhi Development Authority, (2015) 4 SCC 136 (9 January 2015)
authorities.holding: Section 74 awards reasonable compensation for loss caused by the breach; damage or loss is a sine qua non, and where no loss is shown, the named sum is not recoverable merely because it was named.

authorities.cite: Vijaya Bank v Prashant B Narnaware, 2025 INSC 691 (14 May 2025)
authorities.holding: A minimum-service clause requiring Rs 2,00,000 on premature resignation was upheld: it was treated as a genuine pre-estimate of the employer's recruitment and training cost rather than a penalty, and as not being a restraint of trade.

enforceability.plainMeaning: A sum named in the contract sets the ceiling, not the amount. The other side can recover what it can show it actually lost, up to that figure, and a court decides what is reasonable.
caveats: This states the rule in the section. What the other side can actually recover from you depends on evidence a court has not yet seen.
Where the named sum is a genuine pre-estimate of a real cost and is reasonable, courts have allowed the whole of it, as in Vijaya Bank (2025).
Forfeiture of earnest money in property transactions has its own line of cases and is not decided by this row.
Getting money back that has already been paid usually means going to a forum and proving the loss was less than the sum kept.

statute.text: "unfair contract" means a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer, including the following, namely: (i) requiring manifestly excessive security deposits to be given by a consumer for the performance of contractual obligations; (ii) imposing any penalty on the consumer, for the breach of contract thereof which is wholly disproportionate to the loss occurred due to such breach to the other party to the contract.

enforceability.plainMeaning: A deposit that is manifestly excessive, or a penalty far bigger than the loss your breach could cause, is listed in the Act as the kind of term a consumer commission can call unfair.
caveats: Being on this list does not by itself make a term void. A State or National Commission has to declare it so; a District Commission cannot.
The Act protects you only where you bought goods or services as a consumer. Purchases for resale or for a commercial purpose are generally outside it, subject to the self-employment exception.
What counts as manifestly excessive or wholly disproportionate is decided case by case against the facts.
A complaint has to be filed within two years of the cause of action, and you may file where you live or work.

statute.act: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — a model law circulated for States to adopt, not binding law unless your State has enacted it
statute.section: Section 11 — Security deposit (benchmark, not law in most States)
statute.text: The security deposit to be paid in advance by the tenant shall not exceed two months' rent in the case of residential premises and six months' rent in the case of non-residential premises, and shall be refunded to the tenant on the date of taking over vacant possession of the premises, after making due deduction of any liability of the tenant.

enforceability.plainMeaning: The Centre's model tenancy law uses two months' rent as the benchmark deposit for a home and expects the deposit back when you hand over the keys, less what you actually owe. It is a benchmark you can point to in negotiation, not a rule that applies everywhere.
caveats: The Model Tenancy Act is advisory. It binds no one unless your State has enacted its own version, and most have not.
Where it has not been adopted, the State Rent Control Act and the agreement itself govern, and deposit practice varies widely by city.
This row does not say your deposit clause is invalid; it gives you a published figure to compare it against.
Registration rules differ by State. In Maharashtra, for example, every leave-and-licence agreement is registrable regardless of its length.
If a deposit is withheld, the forum — Rent Authority, Rent Controller or consumer commission — depends on your State and on the facts.

forum.name: District or State Legal Services Authority
forum.handles: Free legal advice, drafting and representation by a panel advocate for anyone within s.12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
forum.statute: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, ss.12 and 13

fee.summary: Free, including court fees, process fees and the panel advocate, for anyone eligible under s.12.

forum.filingPlace: At the District Legal Services Authority in your district court complex, which accepts walk-in applications, or online through the NALSA portal.
entitlements: s.12(c) and s.12(f) entitle every woman, every child and every industrial workman to free legal services irrespective of what they earn.
s.12(h) entitles a person whose annual income is below the ceiling their State has fixed, and Rs 5,00,000 applies to Supreme Court matters.
Tele-Law connects you to a panel lawyer free of charge through a Common Service Centre or the Tele-Law app (tele-law.in), which is offered in 22 languages.
caveats: Eligibility is decided by the Authority on the application and the documents filed with it.
Applying for free legal aid does not stop the limitation period for the underlying claim from running.

forum.name: Lok Adalat
forum.handles: Settlement by consent of a pending case or of a dispute before any case is filed, organised by the Legal Services Authority.
forum.statute: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, ss.19 to 22B

fee.summary: Free, and s.21 refunds the court fee already paid when a pending case is settled.

forum.filingPlace: Through the District Legal Services Authority, which publishes the dates of the National Lok Adalat held each quarter.
entitlements: s.21 — an award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court, is final, and no appeal lies against it.
s.21(1) proviso — the court fee paid in a pending case is refunded when the matter is settled in a Lok Adalat.
s.22B — a Permanent Lok Adalat hears public utility service disputes up to Rs 1,00,00,000 and may decide the matter on merits if no settlement is reached.
caveats: A Lok Adalat records a settlement both sides agree to. Apart from a Permanent Lok Adalat under s.22C, it decides nothing by itself.
Because an award is final and no appeal lies from it, what is agreed there cannot later be reopened.
Waiting for a Lok Adalat date does not stop the limitation period for filing from running.
